caption: Thurmaston National School
history:
Standing opposite St. Michael’s Church, on Main Street, Thurmaston's National School opened in 1844, built for the sum of £600 on land donated by Squire Thomas Allen. Weekly church or chapel writing lessons were replaced by a professional curriculum if people were able to afford the 2d fee.
The majority of village children were from poor framework knitting families so bad attendance was commonplace until the fee was abolished in 1891. An extra classroom wing was added in 1869, with separate staircases for boys and girls.
Dormer windows in the upper story and a further extension improved the school by the turn of the century when pupil numbers rapidly increased. By 1925, however, the building was in a poor state. Back yards containing the outside toilets, coalbunker and the air-raid shelters for WW2 had often flooded owing to the proximity of the River Soar. A rise in the school leaving age further added to the difficulties. The two chapels and the Memorial Hall were brought into use as extra classrooms. Roundhill Secondary Modern had drawn away the older children in 1929, but it was not until 1954 when Church Hill Road Infants took the younger ones that the situation eased. A Junior department addition to Church Hill and the opening of Eastfield C.P. School finally closed the doors on the old building to the children of Thurmaston in 1968. The building was then used as an educational Resources Centre and the ‘Old School’ was used for church and community activities. 
The next chapter building's history began in August 2004.  After extensive renovation the Suhradam Mandir (Suhradam Swaminarayan Temple & Community Centre) opened under the Yogi Divine Society, serving local families and devotees.

caption: Thurmaston Working Mens' Club
history:
The first Working Men’s Club began as a Liberal Club in the former Methodist Chapel building in Garden Street. First listed in directories in 1901, it was a place where spittoons would be emptied and the floor swept of its dirty sawdust before fresh was collected from a carpenter’s workshop further up the street.
Indentures dated 1913 name Harry Russell and Walter Strong as mortgagees. Thomas Anthony Clayton, son of a Thurmaston shoemaker, was listed as secretary by 1922. A name change in the 1920s to the ‘Thurmaston Working Men’s Club and Institute’ provided a modern image together with a move to a large new club building near the corner of Cemetery Road (now Hadrian Road).
Beer was kept in a barrel with members helping themselves, being trusted to leave the money for their
drinks. One of the seats was said to consist of a plank balancing on two toilet bases. An extra games room was acquired at the back of the new premises but unfortunately the club went bankrupt.
Housed in an old factory building in Garden Street it re-emerged as the Thurmaston Progressive Working
Men’s Club and Institute with its first balance sheet, dated 1931, revealing beer sales of £25 2s 10 ½d.
The organisation moved to its current home, 805 Melton Road, by 1936 and added an extension and car park facilities during the late 1950s when several old cottages were demolished.
Further extensions over the years have included a lounge named after the first secretary, Thomas Clayton.
The photograph of the c1940 committee was taken in the back yard of this building.

caption: Black Horse, Main Street
history:
The Black Horse was demolished around 1938 and over the following years the site was used for a temporary air raid shelter during WW2, followed by Ryder's Waste Paper Depot and Sunny Textiles, a textile business which burnt down in 2003. Private houses, a car bodyworks workshop and a new complex of flats now occupy the site of The Black Horse and named Black Horse Court.
This picture shows Edward Ballard's name above the door, dates from around the First World War. The cottages to the left, once occupied by the Palmer and Fox families, are up for sale while telegraph poles show the means of communication before the arrival of the telephone in the 1920s.

caption: Black Horse, Main Street
history:
The Black Horse, Main Street looking north.
Picture taken late 1800s with village children and members of the Fox family in front of a thatched
cottage next to the Black Horse pub, with the Wesleyan Chapel and Old Plough pub in the distance.
The Black Horse was a very old establishment, situated opposite the village church of St. Michael's.
A will of 1811 reveals the earliest known tenant of this public house to be William Smith of Sileby, who also kept cattle. For the next seventy years an almost unbroken line of Smith's held the license for this quaint thatched building.
The rooms were very small; upstairs the ceilings were also low and lighting was by paraffin lamps even during the early 20th century. A billiard table and sing-a-longs to a gramophone kept the customers entertained.
The beer was home-brewed supplemented by tea, coffee and sandwiches. Other licensees included Edward Ballard, a market gardener, who kept chickens and pigs in the yard at the rear. The final landlord, George Smith, took the license to the new Manor Hotel in 1938. The Black Horse was demolished shortly after, the site was used for a temporary air raid shelter during WW2, followed by Ryder's Waste Paper Depot and a textile business which burnt down in 2003. Private houses, a car bodyworks workshop and a new complex of flats now occupy the site of The Black Horse.

caption: The Harrow Inn
history:
The Harrow Inn Public House Situated down the southern end of Thurmaston's main street, this public house may have been called the Wellington according to records of 1828, perhaps named after the Duke of Wellington and his battles with the French some years earlier. The landlord was David Bates, who was also a farmer and coal merchant and came from a family of wheelwrights. In 1835 it was listed as The Harrow. Whether his customers preferred farming to wars is not known, but the pub remained in the same family for some fifty years more before it passed through various hands during the 1880s and 1890s.
The photograph above is of Thomas Barrow, who took up the lease in 1912, standing in front of the original premises. Reports of a fire shortly after this date were said to have destroyed the old building shown here, which probably explains why the current one has an Edwardian style facade. The adjoining row of dwellings to the right with its shuttered windows was part of The Harrow yards, a warren of poor worker's houses that have all now disappeared. Pub stories tell of a ghostly figure disappearing through doors no longer there. Evidence of a hotch potch of smaller rooms is revealed by differing heights of ceilings and floors in the modern arrangement, while the skittle alley and the cellar across the old rear courtyards show remnants of the former garden walls.
Shipstone’s began supplying the beverages during the twentieth century, followed by
several others as trade grew. The Harrow Inn 2007 is now a popular haunt with it’s large screen TV, pub games and live entertainment.
